summary.Summary: Nick Morgan (Nutrition Integrated) opened the day by arguing that the principles of sports nutrition have gone further, rather than sports nutrition itself going mainstream, and put three questions to the room: is the category growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries just moving [00:00]. His three rules were that growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, and opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00]. The evidence was Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam (Starbucks say one in seven coffees now carries 15 g of protein), whey protein at historically high prices and the brand responses to it (fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, reformulation, "whey hybrids", whey milkshakes, whey plus collagen at 10 g plus 10 g), creatine moving into gummies, chocolate and products for women, and a hydration market with no agreed electrolyte dose [00:00]. He showed the scale of competition from Nutrition Integrated's tracking: almost 3,500 creatine products, almost 2,800 standalone magnesium products and over 2,500 collagen products, with branded ingredients in over one in two pre-workouts, 40% of longevity products and one in four creatine products [00:00], [18:50]. He closed on "permission to play" and the right to win: everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win [18:50].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India; Starbucks say one in seven coffees currently provides 15 g of protein. "A bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." [00:00]
- Whey protein prices have never been higher and brands are going through a "structural reset", not mitigation: fewer promotions, pack architecture (1 kg to 900 g at the same price), some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines instead. Consumer prices for clear whey, WPI, blends and WPC are up by anywhere between 15 and 25 percent. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00].
- Brands "would love to listen to you about some really good solutions": they want to sell more creatine, electrolytes, pre-workout and higher-value vitamins because the margin structure is better than whey [00:00].
- "Whey hybrids" (presented as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost of goods) launched in greater numbers in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes (whey plus milk) and whey plus collagen (typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks) are the next pillars; GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and air-derived protein are coming through but are still expensive [00:00].
- Plant protein is not taking the gap: ranges come in and out because they still underdeliver on taste. The winning message is "we're just a really bloody good protein", not "plant"; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time and caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00].
- Creatine is now "for all people and for all occasions"; gummies are the fastest-growing format by new launches in the last six months, off a small base, with "lots of conjecture about stability"; "other" formats (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew faster still off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [00:00], [25:59].
- Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack; naturalness (no colours or preservatives, natural sweeteners and flavours, short ingredient lists) is a prerequisite to growth [00:00].
- Product counts tracked: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 standalone magnesium, over 2,500 collagen; longevity small but growing [00:00].
- Branded ingredient penetration: over one in two pre-workouts (many use more than one), 40% of longevity products, one in four creatine products, where most comes from one supplier and "there's a race for those to follow" [18:50].
- Longevity brands and athlete-backed brands (Sergio Ramos linking sport to longevity) compete for the same consumer with sports nutrition products framed as "live better today"; the competitive set has never been broader [18:50].
- Brands must think beyond the category (gut, longevity, GLP-1) but stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and understand the right to win; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
summary.For Vita Actives: Whey margin pressure is the strongest tailwind in the talk for an ingredient supplier: brands are actively looking for higher-margin, non-whey lines and for new protein blends, and he told the room they want to hear solutions [00:00]. For CreaWin: creatine is his benchmark category, one in four products uses a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow [18:50]; my reading is that this is exactly the gap a second branded creatine pitches into, with science and story as the differentiators he named. Gummies and food formats are where creatine launches are growing and stability is the open question [00:00]; my reading is that a stability story for CreaWin in gummies would land with brands. For IsoClr: Pea: his point that plant protein must be sold as a very good protein rather than as plant, and that taste is the barrier, fits a clear pea isolate pitched on taste and clarity first (my reading). The whey hybrid and whey plus collagen trend shows brands will blend protein sources, including in clear drinks, which opens room for a pea component in clear formats (my reading). For Oxystorm: pre-workout has the highest branded-ingredient penetration, over one in two, so it is crowded but receptive to branded actives (my reading). Naturalness and short ingredient lists are a prerequisite across the board [00:00]. Relevance high: it is the market-structure and protein-pricing frame for everything else at this event.

speakers.name: Alan Johnstone
speakers.role: Owner (as introduced; formerly Arla Foods Ingredients)

summary.Summary: Alan Johnstone (owner of Nutrilution, formerly selling whey at Arla Foods Ingredients) explained the supply chain behind this year's whey prices [00:16]. WPI rose from around 7 euros a kilogram in 2023 to over 30 euros earlier this year; WPC80 was stable at around 12 euros until it jumped to 28 euros in about six weeks, which hurt more because brands had already switched into WPC80 [00:16]. Demand is growing at over 10% a year (sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, mainstream protein, clear whey, which is almost all WPI), while liquid whey only grows with cheese production at about one and a half percent a year, and filtration plants are expensive and slow to build [00:16]. Producers have prioritised WPI (growing about 15% a year) over WPC80, and new capacity suggests WPI at 7 to 11% and WPC80 at 4 to 7% a year, but not both at the top [00:16]. Prices overshoot in both directions on buyer behaviour, and right now WPC80 is falling hard while WPI corrects and the substitutes brands moved into (MPC85, caseins, plant proteins) are rising [00:16]. His advice: do not try to time the bottom, keep buying steadily if the price lets you make money, and accept that whey "will be expensive. It should be expensive" [00:16].
summary.Key takeaways:
- WPI went from around 7 euros a kilogram in 2023 to over 30 euros earlier this year; WPC80 held around 12 euros, then rocketed to 28 in about six weeks. WPC80 was the existential risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16].
- Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks is a big underestimate; GLP-1 users as incremental demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); clear whey, which barely existed five years ago, is one of the fastest-selling parts of the category and is almost all whey [00:16].
- Whey wins on taste and texture, not nutrition: "the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source." It is far easier to make a good-tasting product with whey than with most alternatives [00:16].
- Supply: only 0.6% of liquid milk is whey protein; whey comes from cheese, and cheese production grows about one and a half percent a year, so liquid whey does too, against demand growing over 10%. This is his most important conclusion [00:16].
- Factories are the first bottleneck ("phenomenally expensive" and slow to build); liquid whey is the second; byproducts are the third, and WPI producers must also sell a fatty protein stream [00:16].
- Over five years total whey protein supply grew just under 5% a year; WPI about 15% a year at the expense of WPC80, which explains why WPC80 was undersupplied this year. Clear whey may be up to 25% of WPI (top of the estimate range); ordinary instant WPI grew about eight and a half percent, below the category [00:16].
- New capacity: WPI expected to grow 7 to 11% a year, WPC80 4 to 7%, but if WPI is at 11, WPC80 has to be more like 4 because there is not enough whey. Both are below underlying demand [00:16].
- Prices overshoot on behaviour, in both directions (the COVID example): buyers stock up when prices rise and sit out when they fall [00:16].
- Now: WPC80 "has been falling pretty hard", WPI "still expensive, but definitely correcting"; new US factories set in motion three or four years ago are commissioning; producers have better uses for whey (WPI, WPC35, sweet whey powder), so WPC80 production should fall; MPC85 and other substitutes are rising and WPC80 and milk protein lines "should never meet" [00:16].
- Advice: do not try to be too clever with volume; buy steadily if the price works; whey will be and should be expensive; a business that cannot cope with this year's prices needs to change its model [00:16].
- Nutrilution also sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16].
summary.For Vita Actives: The structural case for non-dairy protein is made by a whey insider: cheese grows one and a half percent a year and demand over 10%, and he expects whey to stay expensive [00:16]. For IsoClr: Pea, my reading is that this is the opening, but he also set the bar: mainstream consumers care about taste and texture, not source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good, so a clear pea isolate has to win on taste and clarity before it wins on supply. Clear whey is almost all WPI and is where the squeeze is tightest; a clear pea isolate is positioned exactly there (my reading). The next few months are a window: WPC80 is falling, substitutes are rising and brands have just reformulated, so they are reviewing formulations and open to blends; my reading is that this is the moment to be in front of formulators with pea, before WPC80 settles. Nick Morgan's observation that brands want higher-margin non-protein lines applies here too: CreaWin and Oxystorm are the lines brands want to grow while whey margins are thin (my reading). Nutrilution is a potential partner or competitor in niche ingredients and sourcing advice. Relevance high: protein market structure and pricing.

summary.Summary: Nikki Hancocks (NutraIngredients) chaired a panel on how brands build communities online while regulators watch, opening with an NI report of more than 1,000 misleading food communication posts by influencers, supplements the most frequent subject [00:01]. Sinead Gibbons (Tonic Health) said 99% of Tonic's content is not about its products: the "Unsponsored Truth" supermarket swaps have built 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month, run by one 22-year-old social media manager and a freelance editor [01:00], [14:35]. Julian Harvie (AG1) said too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel, that AG1 practises "restraint", and that Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version" and "a slightly better version" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" [04:17], [18:30]. Dan Richardson (nutritionist) said athletes want the headline, not the numbers, that buzzwords with different connotations from the research are the common slip, and that athletes are the most impressionable audience of all [06:30], [08:33], [32:33]. Luca Bucchini (for ESSNA) listed the rules (the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules, a new digital act coming) and the recurring failures: undisclosed ads, strategies built around non-compliance, and following non-compliant discourse; brands bear most responsibility for influencer claims [09:45], [11:59], [28:27]. On AI, Julian's rule is that the idea must begin and end with a human [35:43].
summary.Key takeaways:
- More than 1,000 misleading food communication posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].
- Tonic's model is "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 20 to 30 second clips, three posts a day, 1.9 million followers, about 70 million views a month, 99% of content not about the product; people come to social "to be educated or to be entertained" [01:00], [03:24].
- Tonic posts 900 pieces of content a month across four channels with a team of one social media manager and a freelance editor; after the ASA pulled up a profile cover claiming "the best sleep supplement in the market" for its magnesium drink, every element now goes through an AI compliance agent [14:35].
- Tonic never deletes a challenged post: it changes the caption, answers the comments, sends voice notes and makes response videos, because "trust is really built in those small moments" [14:35].
- AG1 found that talking about gold-standard trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence does not work top of funnel; the science sits mid-funnel for people in the consideration set [04:17], [18:30].
- Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you"; the approved line was "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
- AG1 cannot associate healthcare professionals, dietitians or doctors directly with the brand, so it uses them for pure education ("what is creatine? Like, how does it work?", "why is magnesium important?") and hopes the credibility transfers [22:46].
- Dan: athletes want the headline backed by research; the common slip is swapping dull research words for buzzwords whose connotations differ, often "genuine accidental misleading"; "what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area" [06:30], [08:33].
- Dan is food first: he told a creatine company's podcast audience that not everybody should take creatine until the baseline of nutrition is fixed, and the company objected [24:22].
- Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": a 35-year-old EFL player with 200-plus appearances bought a supplement off TikTok Shop; they believe "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].
- Luca: the rules are the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules and a new digital act whose text is not yet known; failures are undisclosed ads, no training or allocated responsibility with creators, strategies built around non-compliance, and following a non-compliant discourse [09:45], [11:59].
- Brands bear most responsibility for influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
- Provocation without a solution is fearmongering: Tonic will not post a call-out unless it gives the healthier swap [30:18].
- AI: Julian's hard rule is that "the idea has to begin and end with a human being"; AI scales the middle; he found human copy still better by some margin. Luca expects regulatory action as consumers take nutrition advice from AI agents; AI is also used by regulators to monitor posts [35:43], [38:28], [39:48].
summary.For Vita Actives: Our customers' marketing teams are under claims pressure from the ASA, Clearcast and the claims regulation, and the panel's answer was education content that does not sell: "what is creatine, how does it work" is exactly what AG1 makes with its experts [22:46]. My reading is that a branded ingredient earns its place by giving brands substantiated, claim-safe education they can publish, in the headline-plus-evidence form Dan described, not by giving them stronger claims. For CreaWin, Dan's food-first framing (creatine after the baseline is fixed) and the athlete anecdotes show creatine is already a mainstay in the eyes of athletes and nutritionists [24:22], [32:33]; my reading is that our creatine content should be calm and educational, and wording we supply to brands must survive an ASA review. Luca's point that brands carry the liability for what influencers say means brands will want suppliers' claims to be referenced and hedged exactly [28:27]. summary.Summary: James Morton (Science in Sport) argued that the biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is educational, not biological [00:00]. From a 2021 Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise study of recreational runners with muscle biopsies before and after three sessions, women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished the same; the gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius and disappears when the same absolute carbohydrate is given, so it does not change practical guidance [00:00]. In an England Athletics study of elite runners (marathon bests about 2:20 for men and 2:40 for women) fed 60, 90 or 120 g of carbohydrate an hour over a two-hour run, 120 g prevented the crossover from carbohydrate to fat, exogenous oxidation reached about 1 g a minute at 60 g, 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g and some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took at 120 g, and running economy improved by two to 3% in both sexes; the female data is in second-stage peer review [00:00]. He showed a fuelling matrix from a Journal of Nutrition paper that sets carbohydrate by intensity and duration, from none for an easy hour to 120 g an hour for two to three hours, and described the SiS partnership with Nike After Dark as an education programme in seven cities [00:00]. He does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle: treat the female athlete as an athlete first [00:00]. In the Q&A he said power analysis supports nine participants, fat-free mass may be the better dosing basis for women, and dual-source blends are needed at 90 and 120 g but not below 90 minutes [22:54], [23:48], [24:34], [25:17].
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the 2021 study (recreational runners, 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m, 3 x 10 minutes), women began with less muscle glycogen than men but both finished similarly depleted; the difference was less than 5 g in the gastrocnemius and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
- The gap is a dosing artefact: carbohydrate is prescribed per kilogram, so lighter women take less in absolute terms; given the same absolute amount, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage". His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].
- Elite runners (men about 2:20, women about 2:40 marathon bests) ran two hours after 8 g per kg the day before and 2 g per kg at breakfast; 60 g an hour gave a crossover to fat after about 60 minutes, 90 g shifted it right, 120 g prevented it for the full two hours [00:00].
- Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g some men and women oxidised between 80 and 100 percent of intake, "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported"; men and women do not differ in ability to digest and oxidise carbohydrate [00:00].
- Running economy improved by between two and 3% at 120 g an hour, against Nike's 4% Vaporfly claim; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00].
- Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms than men, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; tolerance may differ slightly, oxidation does not [00:00].
- Fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].
- SiS partnered with Nike After Dark (women's night races in seven cities) on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00].
- "The biggest barrier to fueling the female runner is not biological... it is educational"; under-fuelling is cultural; he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling messages [00:00].
- Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]; women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure [23:48]; 60 g was maltodextrin only, 90 and 120 g dual source; dual source is needed above about 90 minutes and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].
summary.For Vita Actives: Nothing here touches our ingredients: no protein, creatine or pre-workout was mentioned. The value is customer insight: SiS builds its pitch on its own trials (England Athletics, Nike), published papers and a simple matrix, and its chief science voice is openly sceptical of claims he sees on social media [00:00]. My reading is that a sports nutrition brand of this kind expects a supplier to bring trial data and a one-slide rule of thumb, not a benefit list, and that is the standard CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea material should meet. The gut tolerance point (more GI symptoms in women at high intakes) is adjacent to the digestibility story for a clear pea protein (my reading). summary.Summary: Tess Plaquet (technical sport manager, Rousselot) argued that whey prices are here to stay and that the elegant answer is "smarter formulations": replacing part of the whey with collagen peptides rather than raising prices or shrinking packs [00:10]. Her market evidence was whey product launches growing seven and a half percent a year over the last two years, the biggest price growth in 24 to 25 at 8.7, and a tonne of WPC80 going from 5.7k in 2023 to almost 32k in 2026, almost sixfold, with drivers (GLP-1 users, China, active lifestyle consumers, whey being a cheese byproduct, energy, labour, tariffs and climate) that she said will keep prices high [00:10]. Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at almost 17.5 percent a year, often at 10 g plus 10 g, and collagen's supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish with far less price volatility [00:10]. Her science was Rousselot's Peptan studies: 22 men on 45 g whey or 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan for three weeks showed similar recovery and performance; 20 g Peptan with vitamin C for seven days gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster recovery than placebo; 10 g before a 70-minute run held blood endotoxins at the no-exercise level; 8 g a day improved knee discomfort and function in women at three and six months; 15 g a day cut night awakenings from around 30 to 22 and the Peptan group scored 100% on a Stroop test [00:10]. The recording ends mid-sentence as she invites the room to the roundtables.

- A tonne of 80% whey protein concentrate was 5.7k in 2023 and is almost 32k in 2026, almost sixfold in three years [00:10].
- She said the drivers mean "those prices will be here to stay": demand from active lifestyle consumers, GLP-1 users advised to take extra protein, and China; whey is a byproduct of cheese and cannot be scaled easily; gas, electricity, labour, filtration costs, tariffs, geopolitics and climate all push the same way [00:10].
- Three brand responses: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and an opportunity to stand out on shelf [00:10].
- Launches combining whey and collagen are growing at almost 17.5 percent a year; a 10 g collagen plus 10 g whey product was the example [00:10].
- Collagen's supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish and its historical prices show far less fluctuation than whey [00:10].
- Whey is a complete protein rich in BCAAs for muscle building and repair; Peptan is hydrolysed collagen rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline, pitched at ligaments, tendons, joints and bone; "these two are no competitors" [00:10].
- 22 men, 45 g whey against 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan, three weeks of training, jump height and creatine kinase: recovery and performance were similar in both groups [00:10].
- 24 men, 20 g Peptan with vitamin C or placebo for seven days, then 150 jumps: 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo [00:10].

summary.For Vita Actives: Rousselot is selling the same brand problem we sell into (whey cost and supply) with a different answer: partial replacement of whey with collagen, backed by a head-to-head showing no loss of recovery or performance at 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan [00:10]. items.title: Nick Morgan: how longevity is sold, from hallmarks to habits
items.to_check: The recording holds only the last six minutes of the talk, so the billed title, the speaker's organisation and role (Nutrition Integrated is not said in the recording), the five points he refers back to, and the room are unconfirmed.

summary.Summary: The recording catches the last six minutes of Nick Morgan's talk on the longevity consumer. He argued that longevity now sits inside women's health, menopause and sports nutrition, and that consumers connect with "energy and vitality" and "cellular health" rather than the hallmarks of ageing: of about 300 products coded, 9% refer to the hallmarks and, he thinks, only 4% put them in lead copy [00:00]. Brands sell routines, not single products; Solero's AM, PM and two-days-a-month reset was his example [00:00]. Longevity is one of the most expensive categories per serve, and an existing ingredient such as creatine, at a median of around 50 cents a serve, can be made premium by putting longevity on the front [00:00]. Formats are moving beyond capsules (70% of products) into liquids, chocolate, gummies, an NAD energy drink and a spermidine pen, and longevity is moving into hydration and sports nutrition, with Sergio Ramos's brand Centenarian as the example [00:00].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Consumers buy "energy and vitality" and "cellular health"; the hallmarks of ageing are "for this people in this room" [00:00].
- Of about 300 products coded, 9% refer to the hallmarks and only 4%, he thinks, put them in lead copy [00:00].
- "You don't sell one product in 2026": brands sell a routine of about three products, and an ingredient is sold on how it fits the customer's product system [00:00].
- Longevity products are among the most expensive per serve; the creatine median is about 50 cents a serve, and the same ingredient labelled longevity can be "a hell of a lot more expensive" [00:00].
- 70% of longevity products are capsules, but liquids, chocolate, gummies, drinks and injection pens are arriving [00:00].
- Cellular claims are entering hydration, and longevity is shifting into sports nutrition (Centenarian, linked to Sergio Ramos) [00:00].
- Among the ingredients on the longevity shelf he named resveratrol, CoQ10, ubiquinol and spermidine [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives: The clearest point for us is the price gap: creatine at about 50 cents a serve against longevity products that are far more expensive [00:00]. My reading: a CreaWin pitch to brands building a longevity or healthy-ageing line, priced above the sports shelf, is open, and the speaker calls creatine "a daily essential" for himself. His shift of longevity into sports nutrition and hydration is the direction our customers are already travelling, so an AM/PM routine from a sports brand may carry creatine and protein as its daily pillars (my reading). The talk also tells us how brands speak: "cellular health" and "energy and vitality", not hallmarks, so collateral for ageing-focused customers should use their words. Relevance medium: the talk is about longevity positioning, with one direct creatine point.

speakers.name: Miguel

summary.Summary: Miguel (business development) and Brian Keogh (chief scientific officer) of Nuritas, Dublin, presented the company's own AI platform for finding bioactive peptides and the evidence for PeptiStrong, a fava bean protein hydrolysate. The AI takes a mechanism of action or a consumer need and returns candidate peptides for in vitro and in vivo work, about two years from first hypothesis to result [00:20]. PeptiStrong is said to target the mTOR pathway to build muscle and the NF kappa B pathway to lower inflammation; in a murine hind-limb unloading model it prevented 50% of the muscle loss [03:56]. Three human trials were shown: an immobilisation study in the Netherlands against a milk protein concentrate control, where strength came back to baseline and muscle protein synthesis was higher; a 14-day study in a Dublin sports clinic where strength went above baseline within two and a half weeks of a damaging exercise bout; and a KGK trial in Canada in untrained men and women, with faster strength gains at day 28 and 56, lower GDF15 and more bone mineral content [03:56]. Nuritas says PeptiStrong boosts protein rather than competing with it, and could add to creatine, leucine and HMB [03:56]. Claims rest on EFSA protein claims; Vivatis is the partner in Central and Eastern Europe, Nuritas has been active in Poland for six months, and it is developing a product with Tantus [13:50].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Nuritas's proprietary AI goes from a mechanism or consumer need to peptide candidates, then in vitro and in vivo, in about two years on average [00:20].
- PeptiStrong is a protein hydrolysate from fava bean; the speaker says its peptides target mTOR (muscle building) and NF kappa B (inflammation) [03:56].
- Keeping muscles healthy was linked to a 17% decrease in all-cause mortality [03:56].
- Murine hind-limb unloading: PeptiStrong prevented 50% of the muscle loss [03:56].
- Immobilisation trial (Netherlands, males only): the control was milk protein concentrate, not a placebo; muscle lost and regained was the same, but strength came all the way back to baseline and FSR was higher with PeptiStrong [03:56].
- Damage trial (Dublin sports clinic, 14 days' supplementation, isokinetic dynamometer): strength above baseline within two and a half weeks; irisin rose then returned to normal, myostatin was tracked [03:56].
- KGK trial (Canada, untrained men and women, DEXA, supervised training): stronger quicker at day 28, kept at day 56; GDF15 fell with training load; bone mineral content rose, "a kind of a serendipitous finding" [03:56].
- Nuritas positions PeptiStrong as a booster of protein and a partner for creatine, leucine and HMB: "we're not competing with protein" [03:56].
- Claims on pack rest on EFSA protein claims; the regulatory manager has been "creatively defining" others [13:50].
- A library of more than 9 million peptides; next is a non-hormonal sleep peptide, formulated by Vivatis for CEE; six months active in Poland; a development project with Tantus [13:50].
summary.For Vita Actives: PeptiStrong is sold into our customers' muscle, recovery and healthy-ageing products as an add-on to protein and creatine, not a replacement; Nuritas said so explicitly [03:56]. My reading: that makes it a stacking partner for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea in a recovery formula rather than a competitor, and a plant peptide beside a clear pea protein isolate is a coherent vegan story. The trial design matters when a customer quotes it: the Netherlands control was milk protein concentrate, so the headline strength result is against a dairy protein, not a placebo [03:56]. The commercial map matters too: Vivatis distributes in CEE, Nuritas has been in Poland six months and is developing a product with Tantus, which shows which Polish makers are formulating active-nutrition ingredients [13:50]. Relevance high: muscle and protein, a direct creatine synergy claim, and the CDMO relationships behind sports products.

items.to_check: Billed title, Oliver's surname and role, what "MTIC certified" in the UK refers to (Otter's hearing), and the room are unconfirmed.

summary.Summary: Oliver of Kaneka presented ubiquinol, the reduced and active form of coenzyme Q10, which Kaneka makes in Japan. He argued that from about 30 the enzyme diaphorase falls away, so the body converts less Q10 to ubiquinol and should be given the active form directly [00:00]. He cited a blood test in which 90 mg of ubiquinol gave the same blood level as 300 mg of Q10, and said Q10 above 300 mg a day is not converted [00:00]. Kaneka recommends 100 mg a day, up to 300 mg for people on statins, under stress or seeking to have children, and lists heart, energy, mitochondrial, reproductive, cognition and menopause benefits, resting on what he said are more than 100 studies [00:00]. The ingredient comes pure for softgels, gel pills and gummies or microencapsulated for other formats, with halal certification, a partnership with Borussia Dortmund's women's team and a warehouse in Belgium for short lead times [00:00].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Ubiquinol is the active form of CoQ10; the speaker says the converting enzyme diaphorase is no longer available as you get older, from about 30 [00:00].
- 300 mg of Q10 gives the same blood ubiquinol as 90 mg of ubiquinol; at 300, 600 or 900 mg of Q10 the body cannot convert more than 300 mg [00:00].
- Kaneka's dose: 100 mg a day for a normal person; up to 300 mg for statin users, energy, fertility and stress [00:00].
- Claimed areas, the speaker's: immune support, energy, health span, mitochondrial health, heart, male and female reproductive health, cognition, menopause [00:00].
- Formats: pure ubiquinol for softgels, gel pills and gummies; a microencapsulated form for other dosage formats [00:00].
- Made in Japan, more than 100 studies, halal certified, served from a warehouse in Belgium; sponsor of Borussia Dortmund's women's team and "MTIC certified" in the UK [00:00].
- He opened on Nick Morgan's product coding, which placed CoQ10 second among longevity ingredients [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives: Ubiquinol is outside our range and this was a product pitch, so relevance is low. Two things are still useful. Kaneka sponsors a women's football team and lists "energy and sports" among its study areas, so ubiquinol is being pushed into active nutrition as a mitochondrial energy ingredient [00:00]; my reading is that it will appear beside creatine in healthy-ageing active products, not against it. The format note, pure for softgels and gummies and microencapsulated for the rest, is a reminder that our customers' CDMOs want an ingredient grade matched to the dosage form (my reading).
summary.Quotes:
- "You just have to eat 60 avocados or 3.5 kilograms of beef every day to get the daily doses of Ubiquinol." Speaker 1 [00:00]
- "if you take 300 milligrams of Q10, you have equivalent ubiquinol in the blood level when taking 90 milligrams of ubiquinol." Speaker 1 [00:00]

items.title: Aquanova NovaSol micellar delivery, then Balchem OptiMSM

speakers.name: Lena Leder
speakers.role: Senior manager nutrition science

items.to_check: Billed titles, the Aquanova speaker's name (Otter heard "Toshton Sack", the host also "Austin"), the spelling Lena Leder or Leda, the room, and the end of the OptiMSM talk (the recording stops at 12:53, a few minutes in) are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary: Two short talks in one recording. Aquanova's speaker (Otter: "Toshton Sack") presented NovaSol, a micellar encapsulation technology that makes lipophilic ingredients water-soluble: a water-free, homogeneous liquid concentrate in which the native ingredient sits in a micelle with a lipophilic core and a hydrophilic surface, protected from stomach acid, made by physical processing with no chemical change [00:18]. Each formulation is unique to its ingredient; ready products include NovaSol curcumin, astaxanthin and coenzyme Q10, for capsules, shots and combinations [00:18]. His examples were Favea's cap-in-cap product Nourreflex PD and the US longevity brand GVR, which built three products on the same micellar resveratrol plus different NovaSol actives [00:18]. Balchem's Lena Leder, senior manager nutrition science, then began on OptiMSM: Balchem has 33 active research projects across chelated minerals, choline, vitamin K2 and methylfolate [09:04], and MSM is 34% sulfur by weight with evidence, she said, for joint and skin health and exercise recovery [10:40]. The recording ends about three minutes into her talk, before the data.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Attendance: "250" at this edition, as the organiser had announced [00:18].
- NovaSol is a micellar technology: lipophilic core, hydrophilic surface, water-soluble, protected from stomach acid, with no chemical change to the active [00:18].
- Each NovaSol formulation is unique to its ingredient; it is a liquid concentrate for capsules, shots and combined capsules [00:18].
- With enhanced bioavailability "you might need less" of the ingredient per finished dose, the speaker said [00:18].
- Favea uses NovaSol curcumin in the outer capsule of its cap-in-cap product Nourreflex PD; samples were at Favea's table [00:18].
- GVR, a US direct-to-consumer longevity brand, built Mind, Q Power and Glow on the same micellar resveratrol with different NovaSol actives, in vegetarian softgels [00:18].
- Balchem has 33 active research projects; methylfolate is a new ingredient it hopes to bring to Europe soon [09:04].
- MSM is 34% sulfur by weight, a source of sulfur and methyl groups; supplementation "has shown" effects on joint and skin health and exercise recovery, the speaker said [10:40].
- The OptiMSM exercise-recovery evidence was not captured: the recording stops at the start of her science section (my reading of the gap).
summary.For Vita Actives: Neither technology touches our ingredients directly, but both show what our customers' manufacturers are buying. Micellar delivery is a format play: it lets a capsule or shot maker differentiate on bioavailability rather than on the ingredient, and the cap-in-cap and three-product GVR examples are the finished-product systems Nick Morgan described [00:18]. My reading: delivery technology is where a CDMO earns its margin, so when we pitch creatine or clear pea protein to a Polish contract manufacturer, "which format can you make it work in" will come before price. Balchem is a supplier to the same sports and active nutrition brands we serve, and OptiMSM is positioned on exercise recovery [10:40]. Relevance medium for that and for the format lesson.

items.title: Martin Bauer: Rhosera, cultivated Rhodiola rosea against anabolic resistance
items.to_check: Billed title, Ralph's surname and role, the exact name of the new unit (he said "Martin Bauer Nutritions"; Otter heard "Nathan Bawa Nutraceuticals"), the room, and the spellings of the marker compounds and the Polish sites are unconfirmed.
items.added_by: Claude (from Nathan's Otter recordings, 9 Nov 2026)

summary.Summary: Ralph of Martin Bauer Nutraceuticals, a new unit of the family-owned Nature Network (Martin Bauer, Finzelberg, PhytoLab; 4,300 people, over 30 sites, several in Poland), introduced Rhosera, an extract of cultivated Rhodiola rosea aimed at the ageing muscle. His case: by 2050 probably over 2 billion people will be 60 or older; with age the muscle cell uses protein less efficiently (anabolic resistance), which is why protein advice rises from 0.8 to 1.2 g, and hardly any ingredient addresses that gap [00:00]. Wild rhodiola is overharvested, adulterated and, he said, listed as endangered in 2023, so Martin Bauer has cultivated it for 25 years: over 240 accessions reduced over ten years to three elite lines, grown under controlled integrated cultivation in Central Europe, with the root taking three to four years [00:00]. The cultivated material has four to five times the precursor compounds of wild material and, in muscle cells, switches on Pax7, MyoD and polyamine pathways that wild material does not unless concentrated 2.5-fold [00:00]. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75, all training and all given protein, with 400 mg of Rhosera each morning, reduced delayed-onset muscle soreness by 46% in men and 52% in women against 18% and 11% on placebo, and improved chair stand, single-leg balance, bench press, leg press, fatigue and quality of life, "statistically highly significant" by his account [00:00]. Preclinical work is published in Antioxidants and the human paper is in progress; he recommends 250 to 350 mg, and because rhodiola has no EFSA claim, brands borrow magnesium or vitamin B fatigue claims [00:00].
summary.Key takeaways:
- The gap he names is anabolic resistance: ageing muscle uses protein less well, hence the move from 0.8 to 1.2 g of protein, and "hardly any ingredient" addresses it [00:00].
- Wild Rhodiola rosea is overharvested, adulterated with other species and, he said, listed as endangered in 2023: a supply risk for any brand built on it [00:00].
- Martin Bauer has cultivated rhodiola for over 25 years: over 240 accessions to three elite lines in ten years; controlled integrated cultivation with no pesticides and manual weeding; three to four years to harvest [00:00].
- Cultivated material has the same compounds as wild but four to five times the precursors; in muscle cells it upregulates Pax7 and MyoD and polyamine pathways, so spermidine is made in the cell; wild material does the same only at 2.5-fold concentration [00:00].
- Trial: double-blind, placebo-controlled, 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75 with slight muscle loss but no sarcopenia; both arms trained and were given protein; 400 mg once a day in the morning [00:00].
- Delayed-onset muscle soreness fell 46% in men and 52% in women, against 18% and 11% on placebo [00:00].
- Chair stand, single-leg balance with eyes closed, bench press and leg press improved "statistically highly significant"; hand grip was tested; fatigue fell; quality of life and social engagement rose [00:00].

summary.Summary: Alex Glover, who leads Holland & Barrett's global own-label product formulation team, argued that consumers buy outcomes they can feel, not mechanisms [00:25]. He used a tortoise to show that ageing badly is not biologically fixed, and said the category should be about living better, not longer. H&B's data on millions of customers shows repeat purchase goes to products with a clearly communicated benefit (joint function, joint comfort, brain function), and its customer panels talk about playing with grandchildren and getting out of a chair, not sirtuins or telomeres. His evidence against mechanism-led novelty: of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was, and the outcome-level data for nicotinamide riboside and mononucleotide is "very very limited", while cheap interventions (fibre, vitamin D, calcium, protein) have strong evidence; he gave about 9% lower coronary heart disease risk per seven grams of fibre and vitamin D at about two cents per 10 microgram serving. Curcumin, H&B's second best-selling ingredient globally ("one bottle a minute"), was his example of evidence stronger than the permitted claim.
summary.Key takeaways:

summary.Summary: The day's closing panel put a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina), an ingredient developer (Matt), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra) in front of a moderator who asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI. Wants: evidence-based claims and better communication to consumers (Alexandra [02:10]); a "revolution" in clinical trials, with high-dose studies in people with real problems, published so that consumers' chatbots find credible sources (Matt [02:52], [03:45]); a focus on what consumers actually need (Martina [04:30]); and food law as "a shield" for innovators, since the claims system was written for vitamins (Joanna [05:36]). Alex said educated consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording, that brands should do a few claims well, and that H&B starts with the consumer problem and invests in trials and branded ingredients where it wants to win [08:33]. Matt said a new brain ingredient takes three years longer to approve in Europe than in the US, which "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53], and warned of a fish oil supply collapse already hitting aquaculture that reaches shelves next summer [18:48]; Alex described nine months of pre-bought stock and protecting the claim the consumer buys [19:36]; Joanna said "my supplier's fault" is no defence [22:09]. On AI the panel wanted a human in the loop (Joanna [23:33]), peer-reviewed databases (Alexandra [24:59]), and, from Matt, a ChatGPT over factory sensors and "if you can't operate AI... you can't work two years from now" [25:42].

- Matt: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
- Matt: AI assistants rank credibility, peer-reviewed science and university pages, after LinkedIn and Reddit were gamed; the language in published studies matters [03:45], [03:59].
- Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].

- Martina: legislation is an obstacle for a CDMO; do not fill every gap, stick to one piece and explain it; the customer, not the CDMO, has the power to sell [11:13], [12:26].

summary.Summary: Marit Weinstra of HMT, a branding and innovation agency for food and supplements, opened the probiotic programme by arguing that the biotics market (probiotics, prebiotics, fibres, postbiotics) has grown into "a jungle of products" and that consumers say they do not feel informed about probiotics [00:24]. She traced four eras: Yakult's daily ritual and the idea of good bacteria; Danone Activia making digestion benefits tangible, which led to competition on CFU count; a survival era where technology became the story; and the current shift from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut as the gateway to the rest of the body [00:24] [03:59]. From that she gave four rules for winning today: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the whole ecosystem, measurable and felt benefits, and everyday food formats [03:59]. Her evidence was market examples: a US brand built on an Akkermansia strain for metabolic health, fibre brands selling plant diversity, brands setting expectations by week and month, and Poppi as a format consumers like [03:59]. Because most of these claims cannot be made in Europe, she said the brand has to carry them: a "double IP" of rational science plus an emotional brand [03:59].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Consumers say they do not feel informed about probiotics; the category has too many options and not enough clarity [00:24].
- The category was born as a daily ritual in a convenient format (Yakult), then competed on CFU count (after Activia made digestion tangible), then on survival and technology, and now on nourishing the gut ecosystem [00:24] [03:59].
- Rule 1: 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU on shelf means nothing to the consumer; numbers alone no longer build trust, so be the proven expert in a niche, as a US Akkermansia brand does for metabolic health and weight management [03:59].
- Rule 2: talk about feeding what the consumer already has, fibres and plant diversity, which they can see and act on; fibre brands lead this language [03:59].
- Rule 3: early adopters measure with microbiome tests and apps; mass-market consumers keep buying only when they feel a difference, so brands now set expectations for one week and one month [03:59].
- Rule 4: consumers stick with formats they like; Poppi is her example of a product designed around the consumer rather than the ingredient [03:59].
- In Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand must carry them: brand the strain and build a "double IP", rational and emotional [03:59].
- The chair placed HMT as helping companies connect what they can develop with what consumers understand and value [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives: Medium relevance: nothing was said about protein, creatine or sports nutrition, but the branding argument transfers to our customers' categories. My reading: the shift from "what is in the product" to "what does it do for me" is the same shift sports and active nutrition brands face with protein and creatine, and it favours ingredients whose effect a consumer notices, which is how a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea pitch to a brand should be framed. My reading: "science opens the doors, but it's a brand that keeps you in the room" is an argument for branded ingredients with a story a European brand can tell within claim rules. HMT is an agency, not a buyer; it could be a partner for a customer's launch.

- "So in Europe, you can't claim most of it, and that's when the brand has to carry it." Speaker 2 (Marit Weinstra) [03:59]
- "science opens the doors, but it's a brand that keeps you in the room." Speaker 2 (Marit Weinstra) [03:59]

summary.Summary: The recording joins Sacco System's speaker mid-introduction. He presented Sacco as a family company founded in 1872, selling in more than 110 countries, with plants in Como and Milan (the sister company CSL, pharmaceutical API probiotics), a plant in Wisconsin and a pilot for next-generation bacteria in Brisbane [00:00]. He described GMP pharma and GMP food-grade sites, strains screened to EFSA requirements across more than 30 species, a "made-for-you" service developing strains for third parties, and a recent investment in clinical studies and patents in two areas, women's health and healthy ageing [00:00]. CA15, a patented strain isolated from healthy women in 2022, was tested by the University of Catania in an exploratory study of six women and a study of 200 women with bacterial vaginosis and vulvovaginal candidiasis, 10 days of oral intake and a one-month washout; he reported less burning, discomfort, itching, secretions and inflammation and, one month after stopping, 98% with a restored pH range and 92% with a negative amine test [00:00]. Symbio, a 1:1 mix of paracasei and rhamnosus strains isolated from centenarians in the Marche region, was tested in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 97 elderly subjects over six months; he reported more lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and butyrate, a 43% reduction in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, an improvement in IGF-1, which he linked to protein synthesis and muscle mass, and a slower reduction in telomere length [00:00].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Sacco System: family company since 1872, more than 110 countries, plants in Como, Milan (CSL, pharma API probiotics) and Wisconsin, a Brisbane pilot for next-generation and exotic strains [00:00].
- Its pitch as a CDMO is speed and flexibility: a low time to market, working in synergy with the customer, and setting up a new kind of production if asked ("If you have got something crazy, we like to do that") [00:00].
- Offer: probiotics, postbiotics and customised mixtures; "culture science" strains with clinical studies and "culture select" strains screened to EFSA requirements, more than 30 species; strain development for third parties [00:00].
- CA15 (women's health): patented strain, 2022; six-woman exploratory study then 200 women; "10 mil per capsule" for 10 days, one-month washout; he reported reduced symptoms and, one month after intake stopped, 98% restored pH and 92% negative amine test [00:00].
- He said the strain survives the gut, reaches the vagina and promotes the natural lactobacilli while reducing enterococci and Gardnerella vaginalis [00:00].
- Symbio (healthy ageing): 1:1 paracasei and rhamnosus from Marche centenarians; RCT in 97 subjects, "five mil" daily, six months [00:00].
- Symbio results as he gave them: more lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and butyrate, a 43% reduction in hs-CRP ("a marker of inflammaging"), reduced TNF, improved IGF-1 "correlated with the protein synthesis as well as the maintenance of the muscle mass", and "a decrease in the reduction in the length" of telomeres [00:00].
- He used Gemini to find the shoelace metaphor for telomeres [00:00].

summary.Summary: The recording joins Miguel of SPI Pharma mid-talk. He showed three dosage-form concepts: chewable probiotic tablets on a polyol-based, low-water-activity platform (heard as "composol pro tab") compressed at low force so the probiotics survive, with a live product shown under Favea's branding [00:01]; effervescent hydration formats (tablets, stick packs, sachets) stabilised with Effer Soda, a sodium bicarbonate partly transformed to carbonate to form a protective layer, which can also give a "delicate fizz" in chewables and fast melts that distracts the tongue from bitterness [00:01]; and fast-melt (orally disintegrating) tablets for children, elderly people with dysphagia and anyone who dislikes swallowing [00:01]. His close, aimed at the capsule maker ACG: "don't ask your consumer to swallow another capsule" [07:50]. Mihail Jakubowski of Nordic Biotic (a silver sponsor) said the company supplies clinically tested probiotics to brand owners, CDMOs and distributors with full exclusivity by territory at the strain level, and works from genomics to metabolomics (630 molecules measured), functional testing and human studies [09:25]. He presented Northbiotic Mental Balance (Lactobacillus plantarum 140 producing GABA and Bifidobacterium breve 010 producing a B vitamin), tested for eight weeks in 227 students at exam time, 219 completing, with results received the week before; he said statistical efficacy was proved for sleep quality and stress [09:25]. He also showed a microplastic blend of Lactobacillus acidophilus 120 (binds) and Lactobacillus fermentum 160 (pushes away), with a human study in progress and an invitation to a "plastic gut-free initiative" [09:25].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Chewable probiotic tablets: a polyol-based platform with low water content and water activity, compressed at low force, sweet without sugar; probiotics survive the process; shown in a real Favea product [00:01].
- Hydration is a trend in supplements and beverages; effervescence relies on sodium bicarbonate, which with an acid is hygroscopic and unstable over shelf life; Effer Soda is SPI Pharma's stabilised form for tablets, stick packs and sachets [00:01].
- A delicate fizz in chewables or fast melts is also a way to distract the tongue from bitterness [00:01].
- Fast-melt tablets need no water and suit children, elderly people with dysphagia and people who dislike swallowing; SPI Pharma offers an ODT platform that can carry fizz [00:01].
- SPI Pharma's role, as he put it, is creating product concepts so a CDMO can expand into new dosage forms; "we do not limit there" [00:01].
- Nordic Biotic: full exclusivity by territory at strain level; genomics, then metabolomics (630 molecules, "the postbiotics actually"), then functional testing, then human studies; CFU measured to milligrams [09:25].
- Mental Balance: strains chosen for what they produce (L. plantarum 140, GABA; B. breve 010, a B vitamin); eight-week study, 227 students started, 219 completed, "one of the largest study in stress in probiotics in the last decade"; results received last week; he said statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress [09:25].
- Microplastic blend: L. acidophilus 120 aggregates microplastic, L. fermentum 160 pushes it away; offered as a standalone or an add-on to a gut, detox or clean-label formula; the human study is in progress [09:25].
- Nordic Biotic has a GLP-1 companion product with its Swiss sister company Azento; gut-skin, gut-bone and gut-brain technologies were named [09:25].
- WIPO innovation index as he cited it: of 12 countries, seven are European; in the region Latvia, Czechia, Hungary and Poland lead [09:25].
- The chair's aside: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicinal tonic for brain and nerves [08:30].
summary.For Vita Actives: Medium relevance, the highest of the four: formats, not ingredients. Hydration sticks, effervescent tablets, chewables and fast melts are the formats our sports and active nutrition customers sell, and SPI Pharma's platforms are what a CDMO uses to make them. My reading: a CreaWin chewable or fast-melt tablet, and creatine or electrolytes in a stable effervescent stick, are format questions to raise with the CDMOs who work with SPI Pharma and Favea; Favea (shown making a live product) is a CDMO to know. My reading: Nordic Biotic's GLP-1 companion product is the adjacent opportunity for IsoClr: Pea, since protein for muscle preservation on GLP-1 drugs is a brief our customers already have; its stress and sleep blend sits next to recovery positioning in active nutrition. Nordic Biotic's exclusivity-by-territory model is a pattern a branded ingredient supplier can study (my reading). All efficacy claims are the speakers' and the Mental Balance study is unpublished as of the talk.
